title: Organising homework and deadlines
keyIdea: Organising homework means writing every task down with its due date, estimating how long each needs, breaking big tasks into steps, and placing them into a planner so nothing relies on memory alone. Due-soon and high-stakes work gets protected time first; 'I'll remember' and 'easiest first always' are common traps.
familyTip: Once a week, sit with a planner or shared calendar. Write each homework task, its due date, and a rough time estimate. Ask: which ones are due soon, and which need more than one sitting?

lab.caption: Flagship lab: capture tasks with due dates, estimate time, break a project, place work into planner slots, catch memory and easiest-first myths, then challenge.

kid: Start by writing every homework task down. Add the due date next to each one. A list in your head is not a plan — it is a hope.
Guess how many minutes each task needs. If a project is big, split it into steps you can finish in one sitting. Then put each step into a day on your planner.
Give protected time first to work that is due soon or counts for a lot. Fun or easy tasks can fill gaps after the must-do work has a slot.
Two traps: saying I'll remember instead of writing it down, and always doing the easiest task first so the hard due-soon work gets squeezed.
adult: Ages 11–12 Learning to Learn: write homework with due dates, guess time needed, break projects, and use a planner. Nearby lessons cover sorting any jobs (flagtime) and steering one task (flagpme); this one is about a homework list and calendar.
Key words: due date, estimate, planner, steps, protected time. Common mistakes: trusting memory; always doing the easiest task first; skipping time guesses; leaving a whole project for one night.
In the lab the learner writes tasks with due dates, guesses minutes, breaks a project into steps, places work into planner slots, spots memory and easiest-first myths, and practises the plan.

practice.prompt: A solid homework plan starts by…
choices: writing every task with its due date
hoping you will remember later
doing only the easiest task
practice.hint: What belongs on paper or in a planner before you start?
practice.explain: Capture every task and its due date. Memory alone is not a plan, and easiest-first can squeeze due-soon work.

practice.prompt: You have {a} homework tasks and estimate {b} minutes each. How many minutes in total?
practice.hint: Multiply the number of tasks by minutes per task.
practice.explain: {a} tasks × {b} minutes = {=a*b} minutes to plan for.

choices: I'll remember is a solid plan
Break a big project into steps
Protect time for due-soon work
practice.hint: Spot the trap that skips writing things down.
practice.explain: I'll remember is a hope, not a plan. Writing due dates and breaking projects are sound moves.

practice.prompt: A project needs {a}*{b} minutes. You work {b} minutes per sitting. How many sittings?
Due tomorrow: a 30-minute essay. Also: a fun 10-minute worksheet due next week. What first?
choices: protect time for the essay due tomorrow
only the worksheet because it is easier
neither — wait until you remember
practice.hint: Due-soon and high-stakes work gets protected time first.
practice.explain: The essay is due soon and needs more time. Slot it first; the easy worksheet can fill a later gap.

pool.prompt: Why estimate time before you start?
choices: so the work fits into real planner slots
so you can skip writing due dates
so you always pick the easiest task
pool.hint: Estimates turn a list into a schedule you can fit into a day.
pool.explain: Time estimates let you place tasks into planner slots that actually fit. They do not replace due dates or excuse easiest-first.

pool.prompt: Breaking a big project into steps helps because…
choices: each step can fit one sitting instead of one panic night
you can forget the due date
you should only do easy steps
pool.hint: Think about fitting work across days, not one cram session.
pool.explain: Steps that fit one sitting spread the load. The due date still matters, and hard steps still need slots.

pool.prompt: Which belongs on a homework capture list?
choices: task name and due date
only how fun the task feels
only the easiest task
pool.hint: What two facts make a task schedulable?
pool.explain: Task name plus due date (and later a time estimate) make the work schedulable.

pool.prompt: Three tasks need {a}, {b} and {c} minutes. Total minutes to plan?
pool.hint: Add the three time estimates to get a total.

pool.prompt: Always doing the easiest task first is a trap because…
choices: due-soon hard work can get squeezed out
easy tasks never help
planners forbid easy tasks
pool.hint: What happens to hard due-soon work if easy tasks always win?
pool.explain: Easiest-first can burn the evening on low-stakes work while the due-soon essay waits.

choices: capture tasks with due dates → estimate → place into planner
start the easiest task with no list
wait until you remember tonight
pool.hint: List and date first, then time, then slots.
pool.explain: Capture with due dates, estimate minutes, then place into planner slots — especially due-soon work.

pool.prompt: You place {b} equal homework blocks into your planner. Total minutes available: {b}*{a}. Minutes per block?
pool.hint: Total minutes ÷ number of blocks equals minutes per block.

choices: a planned slot kept for due-soon or high-stakes work
only free time after games
time you hope to remember later
pool.hint: Think of a slot you refuse to give away lightly.
pool.explain: Protected time is a planned slot for must-do homework, not leftover hope after games.

pool.prompt: You need {d}*{n} sittings spread over {d} days. Sittings per day if spread evenly?
pool.hint: Divide total sittings by the number of days.
